policy_title: Abolish inheritance tax for estates under £2 million
stated: Reform UK will abolish Inheritance Tax (IHT) for all estates under £2 million, covering approximately 98% of estates, with a 20% tax rate above £2 million and an option to donate to charity instead.

source.quote: Abolish Inheritance Tax (IHT) for all Estates Under £2m That means some 98% of all estates. The rate above £2m will be 20% tax, with the option to donate to charity instead.

bearing_set.reason: Abolishing IHT for estates under £2m increases after-tax wealth transferred to heirs, directly affecting their disposable income; the corresponding reduction in government revenue (IHT raises ~£7bn/year) must be financed through borrowing, other taxes, or spending cuts, each with non-negligible cost-of-living consequences for households broadly.

A substantial reduction/abolition of IHT directly raises the after-tax value of inherited estates for heirs of the ~4-6% of estates currently paying IHT, materially increasing the money they keep — a clear positive verdict on household tax burden.

IHT currently raises ~£7-8bn/year; abolishing it for ~98% of estates and halving the rate for the rest produces a large revenue shortfall that worsens public finance sustainability unless explicitly offset, moving the debt-path indicator in a negative direction.

IHT is one of the few taxes directly on wealth transfer; abolishing it for sub-£2m estates and halving the rate above that reduces a redistributive mechanism, widening the wealth gap between heirs of property/financial assets and those with nothing to inherit — a real worsening of the inequality indicator.

membership_note: Three fundamentals carry genuine verdicts: O11 (tax burden on heirs improves), O12 (public finance gap worsens), O14 (wealth inequality worsens). Effects on O13 (business/farm succession efficiency) are second-order and contested; O1 (property inheritance possibly affecting supply) is too marginal to clear the non-negligible bar.
